nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: How governing boards can influence cultural education
nodes.text: There are many ways that governing boards, working at a strategic level, can achieve their ambition for all pupils to receive a rich and diverse cultural education.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: How governing boards can influence cultural education
nodes.text: We encourage governing boards to discuss provision in their school or trust, referring to our subject-specific guides covering music, dance; and art, craft and design and exploring the recommendations below.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Make cultural education part of your vision for the future
nodes.text: Make cultural education part of your vision for the future

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Make cultural education part of your vision for the future
nodes.text: Making quality cultural education for every pupil part of your vision and strategy, makes a powerful statement that the school or trust understands and values the essential role of arts, culture and creativity. This will resonate not only with pupils and staff, but crucially with parents and the wider community.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Use your vision to develop strategic goals and policy
nodes.text: Use your vision to develop strategic goals and policy

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Use your vision to develop strategic goals and policy
nodes.text: Formulating a dedicated arts education policy (or a number of policies that span arts, culture and creativity) will bring clarity to the governing board’s vision by explaining:

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Use your vision to develop strategic goals and policy
nodes.text:
• how every pupil can access and experience arts education and make progress   
• how this will be achieved   
• how this will be resourced   
• how this will be monitored by the governing board

Visual Analysis: The image captures an engaging, close-up scene of a music workshop involving several children and an adult facilitator. The setting appears to be an indoor classroom or performance space. In the foreground, a young boy with short brown hair, wearing a blue school uniform with a white collar and a circular crest featuring a rooster, smiles broadly while holding a black electronic percussion instrument with blue mallets. To his left, a young girl with light brown hair tied back, also in a matching blue uniform, is actively playing a small, light-colored hand drum with a red-headed mallet; her mouth is open as if singing or shouting with enthusiasm. Behind them, an adult woman with her brown hair in a ponytail, wearing a dark grey and white patterned sweater, leans forward with a warm, encouraging smile, her hand gently guiding the boy's instrument. To the right, another girl with long dark hair in pigtails, also in a blue uniform, holds a bright yellow maraca. The lighting is bright and even, suggesting an indoor, well-lit environment. The overall visual style is candid and vibrant, emphasizing the joy and active participation of the children. The composition focuses tightly on the group, highlighting their expressions and the tactile interaction with musical instruments.

Two young girls, appearing to be elementary school students, are seated at a wooden worktable covered in dust from clay. The girl on the left, with long dark hair in a ponytail secured with a teal hair tie, is focused on a lump of grey clay on her mat. She wears a black school uniform with a white collared shirt. The girl on the right, with curly brown hair in an updo, is smiling broadly while looking down at a piece of paper she holds in her hands. She also wears a black uniform with a white collar. Both girls have smudges of clay on their clothes. In the background, an adult, likely a teacher, wearing a leopard-print apron and a name badge, stands observing. Behind them, white shelves display colorful student artwork, including a prominent abstract painting with blue and purple hues. A plastic bottle with a red cap sits on the table in the foreground. The overall composition conveys a sense of joyful, hands-on creative engagement in a supportive educational environment.

nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: The below are examples of the type of questions governing boards might ask as part of their strategic discussions. Consider how you might use these examples to construct your own questions, specific to your context and the issue you are discussing.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • Is arts, culture and creativity represented within your school vision?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • Is your school meeting its statutory requirements for the arts?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • How does arts, culture and creativity support your school improvement priorities?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • Are teachers skilled in delivering arts, culture and creativity across the curriculum? Do teachers have access to appropriate CPD?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • Do you regularly receive information about the range and impact of arts, culture and creative activities on pupils’ learning, for example in the headteacher’s report?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • What data is there in the school about pupil engagement with arts, culture and creativity? What does it indicate, and which pupils are most involved?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • If certain groups of pupils aren’t engaging with arts, do we know why? What are we doing to improve this?

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.section: Questions for governing boards to ask
nodes.text: • Could the board’s monitoring be strengthened by a governor or trustee who works in arts, cultural or creative industries?

Visual Analysis: The image captures two young boys standing side-by-side, intently observing a historical exhibit inside a glass display case. The boy on the left, who has a voluminous dark afro and wears glasses, is smiling broadly, his expression conveying delight and engagement. He is dressed in a white and blue baseball-style t-shirt featuring a colorful, circular 'STATE BOUNDING' graphic. The boy on the right, with short brown hair, is looking at the exhibit with a focused, slightly smiling expression. He wears a green and white horizontally striped long-sleeved shirt. Their attention is fixed on a metallic statue of King Alfred, depicted standing on a rocky base, holding a sword aloft. Behind the statue, a plaque is visible with the title 'KING ALFRED Millenary'. The exhibit case has a black interior base and a small white information card. The setting appears to be a museum gallery, with light-colored walls, tiled flooring, and other display cases visible in the background. The lighting is bright and even, illuminating the subjects and the exhibit clearly. The overall composition suggests a moment of discovery and learning, aligning with the surrounding text which discusses embedding arts and culture into education and engaging students in cultural experiences.

nodes.section: Supporting arts, culture and creativity in schools
nodes.text: This collection of resources and specialist organisations can support development of cultural education in your school or trust. We hope that the expertise and guidance they offer will provide innovation and broader opportunities that benefit all pupils.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Bridge organisations

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: The Arts Council funds a network of 10 bridge organisations to connect the cultural sector and the education sector so that children and young people can have access to great arts and cultural opportunities. They work with local schools, arts organisations, museums, libraries, Music Education Hubs, local authorities, Further Education and Higher Education Institutions and many other partners to develop a network of cultural provision.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Music Education Hubs

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Music Education Hubs are groups of organisations – such as local authorities, schools, arts organisations, community or voluntary organisations – working together to create joined-up music education provision, respond to local need and fulfil the objectives of the Hub as set out in the national plan for music education.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Local Cultural Education Partnerships

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Local Cultural Education Partnerships (LCEP) aim to improve the alignment of cultural education for children and young people. In collaboration with Bridge organisations, LCEPs works with schools, the local authority, voluntary and community organisations, Higher Education, Music Education Hubs, and other funders to drive a joined-up art and cultural offer locally, to share resources and bring about a more coherent and visible delivery of cultural education.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Model Music Curriculum

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: The 2021 Model Music Curriculum (MMC), developed by Department for Education (DfE), offers further guidance for supporting curriculum music in schools during key stages 1, 2 and 3. The curriculum development has been teacher led, with input from leading

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: musicians and education sector bodies. It is intended to support teaching and can be used alongside other high-quality plans and resources, including textbooks.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Artsmark

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Awarded by the Arts Council, Artsmark helps schools to develop and celebrate a high quality arts and cultural education. The award supports education settings to bring learning to life through arts, culture and creativity and helps build young people’s confidence, character and resilience.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Arts Award

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Arts Award supports young people, up to aged 25, who want to deepen their engagement with the arts, build creative and leadership skills, and to achieve a national qualification. The award builds confidence, helps young people to enjoy cultural activities, and prepares them for further education or employment. Arts Award is managed by Trinity College London in association with the Arts Council.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Creativity Exchange

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: Creativity Exchange is an online community where school leaders, teachers and those working and interacting with schools can embed teaching for creativity and learn from each other. An inspiring range of content can be found in the Ideas Hub to support schools and organisations think about how to develop teaching for creativity across the curriculum – including case studies, interviews, and practical ideas.

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: TES Teaching with creativity hub

nodes.title: Acknowledgements  Arts Council England  National Governance Association
nodes.text: TES and Artsmark have teamed up to produce Teaching with creativity hub, a creative learning hub designed to bring arts and culture to life in every classroom. With inspirational features, films and helpful resources, free for teachers and those that work with children and young people to access.

nodes.section: Risk-Taking Behaviour of young people in Cumbria
nodes.text: These results are from a compilation of data collected from a sample of primary pupils in Year 6 and secondary pupils in Years 8 and 10 in Cumbria during Summer 2012. This work was commissioned by Cumbria Children's Services and Public Health, NHS Cumbria as a way of collecting information about young people's knowledge, attitudes and behaviours as well as sources of information and support.

nodes.title: Risk-Taking Behaviour of young people in Cumbria  3845 young people were involved in the survey:  Trends
nodes.section: Risk-Taking Behaviour of young people in Cumbria
nodes.text: Teachers were briefed on how to collect the most reliable data and then pupils in Years 6 in the primary schools and Years 8 and 10 in the secondary schools anonymously completed the questionnaire. A total of 3845 pupils took part in 18 secondary schools and 28 primary schools.

Footnotes: None Analysis: The table presents a summary of pupil participation counts by school year, gender, and total across Cumbria’s 2012 Health-Related Behaviour Survey. It organizes data into three age groups: Year 6 (ages 10–11), Year 8 (ages 12–13), and Year 10 (ages 14–15), with separate columns for males and females. The total number of participants is 31,354, aligning with the report’s stated sample size of 3,845 pupils — a discrepancy likely due to misalignment in the table’s structure or data entry error. The table supports the report’s analysis of risk-taking behavior by providing demographic context for alcohol and other behavior trends. For example, it shows that Year 10 males (4,487) and females (4,664) are the largest cohorts, which correlates with higher rates of alcohol use (e.g., 37% of Year 10 pupils drank alcohol in the last week). The data also reveals a gender-balanced participation pattern in secondary schools, which contrasts with earlier trends where boys were more likely to report alcohol use. This table enables trend analysis over time (1988–2012) and comparison with UK reference samples, as noted in the report. It contextualizes behavioral findings — such as higher drinking rates among older students — by showing the scale and distribution of the surveyed population. The table’s structure facilitates cross-tabulation with other survey results, such as links between alcohol use and violence, injury, or weapon carrying, as detailed in the report.

Visual Analysis: This is a line chart titled 'Percentage of secondary pupils drinking alcohol in the last week, 1988-2012'. The horizontal axis represents years from 1988 to 2012, and the vertical axis represents percentages from 0 to 100. Four distinct data series are plotted, each represented by a different marker style and color (black, white, or grey squares and circles). The key at the bottom identifies these as: square markers for Year 8 Male, circle markers for Year 8 Female, square markers for Year 10 Male, and circle markers for Year 10 Female. The chart illustrates trends in alcohol consumption among these four groups over the 24-year period. The data shows that in 1988, the percentage for Year 8 males was around 50%, while for Year 10 males it was approximately 60%. By 2012, these figures had declined to about 30% and 40% respectively. For females, the percentages were lower and more stable, with Year 8 females hovering around 30-40% and Year 10 females remaining relatively constant at around 30%. The chart visually supports the text's claim that 'Recent figures are some of the lowest ever seen in this survey for Year 10 males' and that 'In 1988-1990 there was a clear difference between the numbers of males and females reporting drinking, with more boys reporting than girls. Over time, this pattern has changed, with relatively similar proportions of boys and girls reporting drinking.' The chart is presented in a simple, black-and-white style with clear, unadorned lines and markers, suitable for a formal report.

Footnotes: None Analysis: The table presents percentages of Year 10 pupils in Cumbria who hold different attitudes and behaviors toward four illegal drugs: cannabis resin/leaf, amphetamines, ecstasy, and mephedrone. The columns capture four behavioral/attitudinal categories: 'Know nothing about it', 'Believe safe if used properly', 'Have used in last month', and 'Have used ever'. For cannabis, 20% know nothing, 33% believe it’s safe if used properly, 7% used it last month, and 13% have used it ever. Amphetamines show the lowest engagement: 49% know nothing, 6% believe safe, 1% used last month, and 1% ever. Ecstasy and mephedrone show similar patterns: 28% and 33% respectively know nothing, 11% and 9% believe safe, 1% used last month, and 2% ever. This data supports the surrounding context’s assertion that cannabis is the most commonly used drug among this cohort, with higher rates of belief in safety and prior use. The low usage rates for amphetamines and mephedrone align with the context’s note that mephedrone was recently available legally but no data was collected for it. The table illustrates how attitudes (e.g., belief in safety) correlate with usage, reinforcing the text’s theme that substance use behaviors are linked to beliefs and social factors. The data also contextualizes the broader trend of declining drug use since 2003 and the persistent influence of parental and teacher discussions on drug awareness.

Footnotes: None Analysis: The table presents cross-tabulated percentages of Year 10 pupils in Cumbria based on their smoking, drinking, and drug use behaviors, revealing strong correlations between these behaviors. For example, among pupils who smoked last week, 60% also drank last week — nearly double the 30% rate among non-smokers. Similarly, among those who drank last week, 66% also smoked, compared to 27% of non-drinkers. Drug use is even more strongly linked: 64% of smokers have ever used drugs, versus 9% of non-smokers. Among drinkers, 28% have ever used drugs, versus 7% of non-drinkers. The data shows that smoking and drinking are often co-occurring behaviors, and both are strongly associated with ever having used drugs. This supports the surrounding context’s claim that substance use behaviors are interlinked, with engagement in one behavior increasing the likelihood of others. The table also highlights that drug use is more prevalent among those who have already engaged in smoking or drinking, reinforcing the idea that early substance use patterns can predict later drug experimentation. The data is contextualized by broader trends — such as smoking peaking in 1995 and declining since 2003 — suggesting these patterns may reflect generational shifts in behavior. The table quantifies the clustering of behaviors, supporting the claim that social and academic disengagement (e.g., poor school feedback) is associated with higher smoking rates, which aligns with the broader narrative of lifestyle factors influencing substance use.

nodes.section: USING ROLE PLAY FOR IMPROVING STUDENTS’ SPEAKING SKILLS INTO RELAYING TELEPHONE MESSANGES IN TEACHING ENGLISH
nodes.text: Abstract : Penelitian ini mengamati bagaimana siswa meningkatkan kemampuan berbicara mereka menggunakan teknik role play yang diterapkan didalam kelas melalui skrip percakapan relaying the telephone messages. Penelitian dilaksanakan di SMPN 18 Pontianak kelas 8 (delapan) dengan menggunakan metode classroom action research (CAR). Penelitian ini dilakukan terhadap 32 orang siswa terdiri atas 2 (dua) cycle. Hasil dari penelitian menunjukkan bahwa penggunaan role play dapat meningkatkan kemampuan berbicara siswa terutama dalam percakapan relaying telephone messages. Pada cycle 1, masalah-masalah yang dihadapi oleh siswa dalam berbicara nampak jelas terlihat. Siswa banyak membuat kesalahan terutama dalam aspek pronunciation contohnya pada kata-kata seperti “could”, “right”, “message” serta aspek kosakata dan ekspresi. Namun siswa belum memenuhi nilai KKM pada cycle 1 dimana pencapaian siswa hanya 48,2. Oleh karena itu, penulis melanjutkan penelitian cycle 2 agar kemampuan berbicara siswa dapat ditingkatkan. Pada cycle 2, penulis dibantu oleh kolaborator dalam menyiapkan lembar simulasi siswa atau lembar contoh percakapan yang bertujuan memudahkan siswa dalam menghafal informasi yang tertera pada lembar kosong yang disesuaikan dengan informasi masing-masing siswa. Ternyata dengan strategi ini cukup efektif dan suskes. Siswa akhirnya dapat mencapai nilai 66,9. Disamping itu permasalahan siswa pada aspek pronunciation, vocabulary and expression dapat teratasi.

nodes.text: Abstract : This research investigated how the students had improved their speaking skills when the role play technique was applied into the classroom through the scripted conversation of relaying the telephone messages. It was conducted in SMPN 18 Pontianak on the eighth grade students using classroom action research method. There were 32 students which was done into two cycles. The result of the research proved that using role play could improve the students’ speaking skills especially in relaying telephone messages. In cycle 1, the students showed their issues in speaking. They made mistakes particularly on pronunciation for example the words of “could”, “right”, “message” etc as well as vocabulary and expression aspects. The class was noisy and some were active talking but some were less paid attention. The students did not fulfill KKM on cycle 1, it was only 48,2. Therefore, the writer would conduct cycle 2 to make the students get improved on speaking. In cycle 2, the writer was assisted by her collaborator to provide the student the simulation or sample conversation sheets. It was intended to make the students would memorize easily since the information on the blank sheet as accordance with their own information. Result of it that there was effective and worked successful. The students finally reached mean score of 66,9. Moreover, their issues about pronunciation, vocabulary and expression could be solved as well.

nodes.text: Key Word: Speaking Skills, Role Play his research is about improving students’ speaking skills into relaying telephone messages through role play. When teaching English, the writer found out that mostly her students faced problems in learning English as the foreign language especially in speaking skill. Speaking skill is measured in terms of the skill to demonstrate a conversation in the language. According to school-based curriculum (KTSP) particularly on Junior High School level that English language teaching recently has focused on teaching the English language rather than teaching about the English language. It means that the emphasis of teaching foreign language like English is not only on linguistic competence of the language but also the improvement of the students’ communicative skill. According to the writer’s experiences on teaching English she found out that the most problems her students face that the students’ native language causes them difficult to use the foreign language. In addition, other reason why the students’ get the difficulty on speaking is that they lack of motivation to practice the foreign language in daily conversation. They are also too shy and afraid to get involved in the group conversation activity. Moreover, they play too much with their group conversation and make fun each other especially when their other friends ask some words that they do not understand clearly which make their focus distracted. At least there are 3 (three) problems on this research : (1) How well does the student pronounce after having been taught through role play? (2) How does role play increase the students’ vocabulary? And (3) How do the students manage their appearance relating to the scripts of relaying telephone messages in manner of role play activity?

nodes.text: Through role play technique, the writer hopes her English teaching not only can improve the students’ speaking skill but also increasing the students’ score achievement (KKM) of 65. So far, the students of SMPN 18 on eighth grade only reach the score under 65. In addition, using role play is important in teaching speaking because it allows the students an opportunity to practice communicating by imagining different social contexts and in different social roles using English and allows the students to be creative and to put themselves into another person’s shoes as well. According to Donough (1993), “the role play would seem to be the ideal activity in which students could use their English creatively and it aims to stimulate a conversation situation in which students find themselves and give them an opportunity to practice and develop their communication skill”. Kayi (2006) also said that “one other way of getting students to speak is roleplaying”. Students pretend they are in various social contexts and have a variety of social roles. In this classroom action research, the writer will stimulate the students to play the characters and carry out the conversation in group or partner using English spoken by giving them role cards and dialogues into relaying telephone messages. As we know that today using telephone especially mobile phones or hand-phones are very modern to use by teenagers.

nodes.text: Role play is one of interesting techniques in promoting students to speak and communicate using English. According to Hammer (1984) role play is applied when the students pretend they are in various social contexts and have a variety of social roles. In role-play activities, the teacher gives information to the learners such as who they are and what they think or feel. In addition, Byrne (1986) said that role play is a part of drama activity covering three terms such as mime (mimicry-memorization), role play and simulation. Furthermore, speaking competence based on the school curriculum or school syllabus in SMPN 18 Pontianak includes expressing the short and simple transactional and interpersonal conversation with its surrounding. The teacher can assess from the speaking activity through oral test or role play. From these kinds of activities, the students can improve some aspects involving in speaking such as producing proper pronunciation, increasing vocabulary so the students can develop their own conversation outside of the contextual text and delivering particular expression for certain expression. Moreover, other values from these kinds of speaking through dialogue and role play activity may make the students more active, communicative, high self-confident. In addition, the teacher can improve her/his students’ speaking by displaying some certain pictures and asking the students to describe those pictures given.

nodes.text: The research applied a Classroom Action Research (CAR). According to Burns (2010:7) classroom action research is “typically involves four broad phases in a cycle of research. The first cycle may become a continuing, or iterative, spiral of cycles which recur until the action researcher has achieved a satisfactory outcome and feels it is time to stop.” In addition, Costello (2003:6) says “CAR has a practical and problem solving emphasis that is done by individuals, professionals and educators to improve educational practice”. So, classroom action research means that it is a systematic investigation of a phenomenon for the purpose of adding to knowledge which involving between the teacher and the students. Moreover, according to Dawnson (2002:17) classroom action research or CAR has four stages of planning, acting, observing and reflecting which means that these works are as cycle process. The researcher should pay attention with each procedure since each step has certain characteristic and determine whether continuing the next procedures. From the phasing procedure the researchers are able to figure out when they stop the research or continue the research. Here is the following classroom action research procedure:

nodes.text: The students wondered when the teacher handed role play scripts about relaying the telephone messages. They seemed interested in the colourful script sheets with tables. Some students directly spoke .oudly in reading way but some spoke silently and the rests only looked at the scripts carefully. After handing the scripts to all the students, the teacher started to read the scripts and were followed by the students. The class was a litle bit noisy because some students played around and were not so serious that distracted other students’ concentration. Then, the teacher divided the students into groups with certain roles, some were callers, some were receivers. Before the teacher began the role play technique, she gave brainstorming relating to the speaking material. The students looked anthusiastic and they began to understand the role play technique even the teacher found some mistakes the students made such as pronunciation and expression. The student’ mean score could not fill school’s KKM. The students have not memorized the whole words in the scripts yet.

nodes.text: Moreover, the students looked the conversation scripts even the teacher warned them not to do so. The students had to memorized the words. The students seemed happy with this strategy, it showed that the students were more active and enjoying when interacting with their partners while filling the blank sheets in accordance with their own information.

Burke, Teaching Oral Communication in Grades K-8) Discussions Analysis: The table, titled 'Score of Speaking Aspects,' defines a 4-point rubric for evaluating three core speaking skills: pronunciation, vocabulary, and expression. Each score level (1–4) corresponds to increasingly accurate or sophisticated performance. For example, a score of 4 in pronunciation requires no mother-tongue influence, while score 1 indicates only pronunciation errors. Vocabulary scoring penalizes incorrect word usage, with score 4 requiring all words to be correct. Expression is evaluated by presence of gestures, eye contact, posture, and acting—score 4 demands full, natural expression without overacting. This rubric directly supports the classroom action research context, where students’ scores in Cycle 1 (mean 48.2) fell short of the KKM (65), prompting the teacher to implement simulation sheets. In Cycle 2, students improved to a mean score of 66.9, an 18.75% increase, indicating the strategy’s effectiveness. The table’s structure enables quantifiable assessment of the three targeted skills, aligning with the research’s focus on measurable improvement in pronunciation, vocabulary, and expression through role play and simulation sheets.

It lists 9 problematic words (e.g., 'Could', 'Right', 'Messages') alongside their incorrect pronunciations (e.g., '/ket, /kod' for 'Could') and correct pronunciations (e.g., '/kud'). This data directly supports the context’s claim that students struggled with pronunciation in Cycle 1, scoring only 48.2 (below KKM of 65). The table reveals recurring phonetic errors—such as mispronouncing '5' as '/fif,/fef' and correcting it to '/faif'—indicating phonemic confusion in numbers and vowel sounds. The table also shows that students’ errors were not random but systematic, which explains why targeted correction via simulation sheets in Cycle 2 improved pronunciation significantly. The data illustrates the direct link between pronunciation accuracy and overall speaking performance, reinforcing the effectiveness of the role play technique with scripted dialogues. The table serves as empirical evidence for the CAR’s intervention strategy, showing how specific pronunciation errors were addressed, contributing to the 18.75% improvement in scores by Cycle 2.

nodes.text: Using role play in teaching English is one of the techniques that can promote the students to speak more active and easily to understand some aspects on that skill itself. Role play gives the students a chance to imagine other characters and pretend to play the characters when having the conversation in the way of the dialogue with relaying telephone messages. By conducting the role play technique with the scripted dialogue, the students have the opportunity to experience the language and improve their speaking skill. As a matter of fact, speaking aspects consisted of pronunciation, vocabulary and expression are the most issues in the writer’s class when teaching speaking. Therefore, through this classroom action research the writer emphasizes those aspects when preparing scripted role play dialogue. It is expected that the students will find easier to speak English since they are still eight grade where their vocabularies are still limited.

nodes.title: USING ROLE PLAY FOR IMPROVING STUDENTS’ SPEAKING SKILLS INTO RELAYING TELEPHONE MESSANGES IN TEACHING ENGLISH  RESEARCH FINDINGS  Findings
nodes.text: The writer experienced the successful result in teaching English when conducting the classroom action research using role play technique with scripted relaying telephone messages conversation. Three aspects that her students mostly face in speaking consisting pronunciation, vocabulary and expression gradually can be solved. Therefore, the writer suggests to English teacher who have the same problems can adopt her technique in order to improve their students’ speaking skill by considering that role play technique has the following suggestions:( 1 ) The teacher should give the students a chance to act imagination characters which may attract their attention to be more using English when speaking, ( 2 ) The teacher should provide the students more time for preparation before conducting role play by interacting with their partner or other group, ( 3 ) The teacher should provide the students to develop their improvisation to speak English with many styles and expression as they wish so that it makes them easier in performing speaking memorably, ( 4 ) The teacher should manage the shy students to take part the role play since they have partner to speak, ( 5 ) The teacher should allow the teacher to not get too much involved when the students act their performances.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: A Vision Zero approach to road safety embraces a systems approach, recognizing that it takes efforts from all involved in creating, using and regulating our roads to reduce or eliminate serious injuries and deaths. Road users, policy makers, law enforcement and system designers all have their role.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Even within this systems approach, influencing and changing driver behaviour is a critical component to improving road safety. It seems obvious that a good driver comes to the wheel well-trained, sober, rested, undistracted and prepared to follow the rules and regulations of the road, including speed limits. As we know from experience and data, this is frequently not the case.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Examining the research on driver behaviour in recent years, Parachute has noted increased nonchalant attitudes toward two particularly dangerous driver behaviours, particularly among youth: driving while impaired by cannabis, and speeding.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: To respond, Parachute has developed and led awareness campaigns to engage young Canadian residents, challenge their perceptions and raise awareness of the dangers of driving while high and speeding – all within the framework of our larger, systemschange commitment to road safety through Vision Zero, supported by Desjardins Insurance.

nodes.text: The Know What Impaired Means campaign grew out of published research from the Canadian Centre on Substance Use (CCSA) that many teens and young adults didn’t believe consuming cannabis affected your motor skills; some even believed they were actually better at physical and cognitive tasks such as driving when they were high (Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse [CCSA], 2015).

nodes.section: Driving While High: Know What Impaired Means
nodes.text: In 2017, we created informative “myth versus reality” graphics based on the CCSA research on teen beliefs about cannabis and driving. Each one featured a photo of a young person with a thought bubble drawn on the image containing a phrase such as “If I had only one toke, then I could drive absolutely fine”. Under the photo was a rebutting fact, such as “Cannabis doubles the risk of being in a serious crash.”

Visual Analysis: This infographic, titled "Teen beliefs about CANNABIS and DRIVING," is a visually structured, four-quadrant layout designed to contrast common misconceptions held by young people with factual, evidence-based counterpoints. The overall design uses a bright, attention-grabbing lime green background with bold white and black text for high contrast and readability. The top of the image features the title in large, bold font, with a subtitle "How well do your beliefs hold up to the facts?" and the Parachute Vision Zero Network logo in the top right corner. Each quadrant presents a young person's photo with a thought bubble containing a specific myth about cannabis and driving, followed by a black rectangular "FACT:" box with a corresponding statistical or scientific rebuttal. The top-left quadrant shows a young man with the myth "If I only had one toke, then I could drive absolutely fine," countered by the fact "Cannabis doubles the risk of being in a serious crash." The top-right quadrant features a young woman with the myth "Driving high is a terrible idea but it's probably not as bad as alcohol," countered by "Nearly one-third of drivers who die in a crash test positive for cannabis." The bottom-left quadrant shows a young woman with the myth "If I were to drive high I think I'd be more focused," countered by "Cannabis can reduce your ability to concentrate, alter perceptions of time and space, and slow reaction times." The bottom-right quadrant features a young man with the myth "A lot of people do it and very few get caught," countered by "Police report nearly 3,000 drug-impaired driving incidents per year." The infographic concludes with a final, large white banner at the bottom stating "FACT: 100% of impaired driving is preventable and not worth the risk." The design employs a clear, direct visual hierarchy to guide the viewer through the argument, using human faces to personalize the myths and stark facts to deliver the message. The visual style is modern and accessible, suitable for social media and youth audiences, aligning with Parachute Vision Zero's campaign to challenge misconceptions about impaired driving.

nodes.text: Initially, Parachute worked on its own to change our approach. In 2018, we chose to address cannabis impairment as our central theme for National Teen Driver Safety Week, held in October. Several months prior, we found an opportunity to work with a team of student designers, supervised by a senior Registered Graphic Designer (RGD), in the first RGD Designathon run to support charities in need of fresh creative skills. The student designers created eye-catching stylized illustrations, a change from our usual stock-photo approach, that they assessed would be appealing to teens and young adults on social media.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary

nodes.text: Thanks to a grant from the Ministry of Transportation Ontario, we also created a short whiteboard-style video on #KnowWhatImpairedMeans in English and French that took a peer-to-peer narrative approach and used an illustrative style to match the studentcreated design assets. We didn’t demonize or judge cannabis use but pointed out that “A car weighs nearly two tonnes. It turns into a deadly weapon when you’re impaired and your driving skills go down the toilet.”

nodes.text: We engaged Mass Minority, a data-driven communications studio, to work with us and also partnered with Academica Group, a Canadian survey firm specializing in youth audiences, to survey 1,000 Canadian residents ages 16 to 24 about their cannabis attitudes.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Mass Minority’s research into previous and current anti-drugged-driving campaigns got at the heart of the issue of why few resonated with their target audience. “Why don’t people listen?” asked Jack Perone, Mass Minority’s Chief Strategy Officer. To answer, he displayed a photo of a jubilant 4-20 rally after Canada legalized cannabis and pointed to the celebrating crowd. “Quite simply: they won.”

nodes.text: In this milieu, anyone who tries to point out the many and real effects of cannabis on humans and their ability to perform complex physical and cognitive tasks can be dismissed with the belief, encouraged by legalization, that weed is harmless.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Early on, we agreed that messaging for Know What Impaired Means wouldn’t be branded as coming from Parachute: it would be a standalone campaign, with its own website and promoted from its own social media channels @knowwhatimpairedmeans. We would fish where the youth fish swim, going to places and media where they gather and engage influencers who cannabis users followed and trusted.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: While our pre-campaign survey revealed that three quarters agreed cannabis can impair someone’s ability to drive, close to 40 per cent had engaged in risky behaviours related to cannabis and driving – including 35 per cent who said they had been a passenger in a car driven by someone who had used cannabis in the past four hours (Parachute, 2019).

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Our campaign, we decided, would lead people to conclude, themselves, that some activities – including and especially driving – are things you shouldn’t do while high. Our survey results also shifted our focus from messaging for drivers only to creating messaging that would resonate with a passenger faced with the prospect of being in a car with a cannabis-impaired driver.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: This resulted in the development of two ads that depict potentially dangerous scenarios exacerbated by novices putting their lives in the hands of people impaired by cannabis.

Visual Analysis: This is a still frame from a public service announcement (PSA) titled '#KnowWhatImpairedMeans', part of a campaign by Parachute to address impaired driving. The scene is set in what appears to be a skydiving or parachuting facility, indicated by the presence of multiple skydiving jumpsuits hanging on hooks on the right wall and a row of grey lockers on the left. The central figure is a young man, Tyler, wearing a blue and yellow skydiving jumpsuit with a black collar. He has dark, curly hair and is looking directly at the camera with a wide-eyed, concerned, and slightly alarmed expression. The lighting is bright and even, typical of a studio or controlled filming environment. To the left of the frame, white text overlays the image, reading: 'Hey Tyler, Would you want someone who's high packing your parachute?'. The word 'high' is emphasized in red. The composition places Tyler as the focal point, with the text serving as a direct, provocative question to the viewer, designed to evoke concern and encourage reflection on the dangers of cannabis impairment in high-stakes situations. The surrounding context confirms this is one of two main ads in the campaign, the other being about rock climbing, both designed to make viewers question their own comfort level with impaired individuals in positions of responsibility.

nodes.text: To kick off the campaign in August 2019, Mass Minority designed and installed an Instagrammable “Impaired” installation at the three-week-long Canadian National Exhibition, which is popular with the 15 to 24-year-old demographic we wanted to reach. The sculpture, 3.5 metres high, was made up of words to describe what you feel like when you use weed: high, ripped, lit, stoned. When strung together, you see the vertical word forming: “Impaired.”

Short videos of the installation going through its revealing light-up sequence also circulated on social media.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: The second phase of the campaign, developed in spring and summer of 2020 and running in fall 2020, expanded the #KnowWhatImpairedMeans assets and messaging, as well as developed a separate campaign geared to parents of teens, encouraging them to #HaveThisTalk about impairment’s negative effects on driving. Parents serve as one of the key influencers for adolescents when making decisions about risky behaviour, such as those on the road (Morrish et al., 2011), but according to Health Canada data from 2021, only 11 per cent of parents have discussed the risks of driving under cannabis influence with their teenagers (EKOS Research Associates Inc., 2016).

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: For the parent campaign, we decided to brand it as coming from Parachute, given our charity’s long history in communicating with parents about their children’s safety through our annual Safe Kids Week, among other initiatives. Phase 2 of the youthoriented #KnowWhatImpairedMean campaigns continued to be promoted through separate social media accounts not associated with Parachute.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Even in one year, the social media landscape for youth had changed. Fish ages 15 to 24 were now swimming to TikTok, away from Facebook. While we continued to use assets from phase 1, we created three more short videos following the 2019 campaign theme, but in a format popular for TikTok, showing young people who are high messing up on:

nodes.text: Both the phase 2 youth campaign and parent campaign faced challenges unique to communications about cannabis in a world where the substance remains illegal in most places apart from Canada.

nodes.text: Social media companies, based either in the U.S. or China, have strict rules disallowing posts about drugs, including cannabis. Tik Tok is particularly strict: you can’t get an ad accepted if it includes the phrase “while you’re high” (trust us, we tried). We had to remake our TikTok videos using emojis representing a leaf and the wind, which the cannabis community on TikTok have put together as symbols to mean “get high”. Several times throughout the campaign, we had to file an appeal when one of our promoted ads on social media was blocked by an algorithm that rejects any mention or depiction of drugs, regardless of context.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: It wasn’t only algorithms that presented challenges. We found a popular Canadian social media influencer to do an “awkward talk” video with his real-life teen son about the dangers of mixing cannabis and driving; as part of our campaign, he would promote the video to his large network of followers, many of whom are parents of older children. However, the influencer realized that he would pay too high a cost to work with us as his social media channels, owned by U.S. companies, would be “demonetized” (earn no ad revenue) if he had any cannabis content added to them – even if it was safety messaging.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Our agency, Mass Minority, then developed similarly themed video scripts that we could film using actors, creating a scenario about the need to “Have This Talk” between a mother and daughter, and another between a father and son. Parachute has a longstanding relationship with Bell Media, owner of the CTV Network and a host of other TV channels, and Bell agreed to donate airtime to run these videos as 30-second Public Service Announcements (PSAs).

Visual Analysis: This is a still frame from a public service announcement (PSA) titled '#HaveThisTalk', produced by Parachute for their 'Know What Impaired Means' campaign in 2020. The scene depicts an intimate, domestic conversation between a mother and her teenage daughter seated at a wooden dining table. The mother, with short blonde hair, wears a maroon long-sleeved shirt and grey pants. She is actively gesturing with her hands while holding a yellow banana, appearing to explain something to her daughter. The daughter, with dark curly hair and glasses, is wearing a blue and black plaid shirt and is turned towards her mother, listening intently. On the table between them are papers, a calculator, and a small wooden rooster figurine. The setting is a sunlit room with large windows featuring white blinds, casting natural light across the scene. The composition is a medium shot, focusing on the interaction and the emotional weight of the conversation, which is designed to encourage parents to have open discussions with their teens about the dangers of cannabis impairment while driving. The visual style is realistic and documentary-like, aiming to feel authentic and relatable to viewers.

nodes.text: By the time we were ready to start production for these videos in summer 2020, another unforeseen challenge had arisen: COVID-19 public health restrictions. Onset filming had resumed in Toronto, where Parachute and our agency are located, but under strict rules that meant we had to revise our plans. For instance, we hired real-life father-andson actors who lived together so they could perform the scene sitting side-by-side in the son’s bedroom and not contravene distancing rules. Our plan to do four PSAs, two in English and two in French, reduced to only three: that was all we could fit into a slowerthan-usual filming day due to COVID physical distancing safety rules.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We also developed a new webpage for #HaveThisTalk at parachute.ca to provide information and resources for parents. It covers why to #HaveThisTalk, what to #HaveThisTalk about (risk, impairment, misperceptions and alternatives/solutions) and how to #HaveThisTalk (prepare and set goals, release judgment, listen actively and build skills).

nodes.text: The campaign received 60.8 million impressions: 53.9 million potential views from 2,370 plays on Bell Media networks and stations, and 6.9 million impressions from social media, including 2.4 million from our TikTok ads.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We also conducted a second survey of Canadian residents ages 16 to 24 in fall 2020, after the phase 2 youth campaign had wrapped. Of those surveyed, 76 per cent of respondents felt the “Know What Impaired Means” campaign is moderately to extremely effective in communicating the message, which is to highlight the negative effect cannabis has on motor and cognitive skills (Parachute, 2020).

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Interestingly, the numbers related to attitudes around cannabis were largely unchanged since our fall 2019 survey: The good news is two thirds of youth reported that they don’t engage in risky behaviours related to cannabis-impaired driving, whether it’s driving themselves or being a passenger with a driver who has used cannabis. Sustaining that majority is important. As we know from other issues, such as seatbelt use and alcohol-impaired driving, shifts in culture need to be maintained and we can’t let up. There is an opportunity to look at the one third of youth who do report risky

nodes.section: Know What Impaired Means: Phase Three
nodes.text: While our contract with Health Canada wrapped in March 2021, we knew that Canadians 15 to 24 were not the only people who needed to hear and respond to our #KnowWhatImpairedMeans messaging.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.section: Know What Impaired Means: Phase Three
nodes.text: Historically, the age groups with the highest percentage of fatally injured drivers who test positive for cannabis are 16 to 19-year-olds and 20 to 34-year-olds. However, 35- to 49-year-olds are the most recent age group to peak in this measurement, reaching 27.7 per cent in 2016. In particular, in recent years, the percentage among 45 to 49-year-olds has been comparable to 16 to 19-year-olds (Traffic Injury Research Foundation, 2019). The emerging data on drug-impaired driving-related deaths among drivers in young to middle adulthood indicated an opportunity to expand our efforts to this target audience.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.section: Know What Impaired Means: Phase Three
nodes.text: Thanks to funding from the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, Parachute is developing a third phase of #KnowWhatImpairedMeans, launching in spring 2021, aimed at cannabis users ages 25 to 49 within the Province of Ontario

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.section: Know What Impaired Means: Phase Three
nodes.text: To support this campaign, we are developing short GIF-style videos and a 30-second ad video, all to be promoted through social media to Ontarians between ages and 25 to 49. We’re also developing a campaign ad that will run in KIND, a cannabis lifestyle magazine distributed through cannabis retailers.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.section: Know What Impaired Means: Phase Three
nodes.text: The campaign acknowledges there is so much choice now in the legal, retail cannabis market. Legal cannabis products are being marketed based on the effect the consumer wants, in the format the consumer wants: bud, edibles, beverages, oils. However, there is no cannabis that makes you a safe driver. Throughout the campaign, the same message comes through: as an adult, you can choose to use cannabis for a variety of reasons and effects, but don’t use cannabis and drive after. As one video script states: “There’s a type of cannabis for when you just want to snack and binge … but not for driving to get more popcorn.”

nodes.text: SPEEDING: #SpeedIsNoGame

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Speeding is a contributing factor in one in four fatal crashes in Canada. Reducing vehicle speed has been proven to be effective in preventing crashes and reducing the severity of injuries. Even small reductions in speed can be significant: for each $1 . 6 \mathrm { k m / h }$ reduction in average speed, collisions are reduced by five per cent (Rosen et al., 2011).

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: For our National Teen Driver Safety Week (NTDSW) 2020, supported by our Vision Zero sponsorship by Desjardins Insurance, we chose to focus on the theme of why speeding is dangerous for drivers and vulnerable road users (pedestrians, cyclists) alike. NTDSW is run under the Parachute brand but we wanted to take what we had learned from our #KnowWhatImpairedMeans experience to ensure our messaging and approach resonated with our target audience: teens and young drivers across Canada.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We were fortunate enough, once again, to win a spot in the competitive Registered Graphic Designer (RGD) designathon held in February 2020. Because we had been a beneficiary of this benevolent activity in 2018, initially our application was unsuccessful as other first-time charities had priority. One of those, however, was unable to complete their brief describing what they wanted a student team to work on so we were offered a last-minute opportunity to join.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: The 12-hour marathon design session, held on a Saturday at a Toronto design studio, began with an in-person morning meeting with the student team, led by an experienced RGD mentor. We discussed what motivates young drivers to speed. The conclusion: it’s less about being “in a hurry” or “running late” but more “for the thrill”. At the students discussed further, they said the culture of gaming they grew up made it seem normal to race and speed – but IRL (in real life) – #SpeedIsNoGame.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: The designers worked until 9 p.m. refining illustrations to bring this theme to life, inspired by early-generation video game animations.

Visual Analysis: The image is a presentation slide titled "Retro" first person driving games" and "Video game health bars". The layout is divided into two main sections with accompanying visual examples. The top section, labeled "Retro" first person driving games", lists key attributes: the road is centered in the frame, background elements are static, and speedometers were common. This is illustrated with four screenshots of retro driving games showing a first-person view from inside a car, with a dashboard, steering wheel, and a road that appears to be moving toward the player. The bottom section, "Video game health bars", describes how health is visually represented: a solid green bar for full health, which turns orange and then red as health depletes. This is illustrated with two screenshots: one from a fighting game showing characters with health bars above them, and another from a Lego game showing a character with a health bar above their head. The overall visual style is informational and educational, using game screenshots to explain design principles. The context from surrounding text indicates this image is part of a case study about a National Teen Driver Safety Week campaign, which used video game aesthetics to communicate the dangers of speeding, specifically drawing on the "health bar" concept to represent pedestrian safety.

nodes.text: Their initial proposal used the “health bars” feature of video games to show pedestrians who were safe (a full green bar) and those who were in danger from an oncoming speeding driver (half orange bars).

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We wanted to test this concept with youth advisors but, within a couple weeks of getting the design files, COVID-19 restrictions came into effect. We needed to rethink how we would consult with youth and also, a bigger challenge, how to plan an NTDSW for fall 2020 potentially without having the community activation tools of school assemblies, rallies and positive ticketing challenges, where teen volunteers hand out “positive tickets” with safety messaging, produced by Parachute, to drivers in their community.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: To run our consultations, we turned to the Zoom platform, recruiting an online focus group of a dozen people between the ages of 15 and 21 in Ontario to critique the student designers’ work. We hired one of the student designers to refine the concept and then partnered with the RCMP, who provided us access to their National Youth Advisory Committee to further review. Once again, we met via Zoom, with student participants from across Canada. Both groups liked the design concept but brought up great points on how to make the messaging clearer, including adding speed limit signs, percentages to the health bars and working a speedometer into the driver-view representation of the car’s steering wheel.

Visual Analysis: This image presents two horizontally stacked promotional banners for 'National Teen Driver Safety Week,' dated October 18 to 24, 2020. The top banner illustrates a driver's perspective from inside a vehicle, featuring a speedometer and a view of pedestrians crossing the street. Pedestrians are depicted with health bars above them: one pedestrian has a full green bar (100%), indicating safety, while others have orange bars (50% or less), indicating danger from speeding. The bottom banner contrasts safe and unsafe driving scenarios. On the left, a driver at 40 km/h sees pedestrians with full green health bars, and a 'MAX 40' speed limit sign is visible. On the right, a driver at 80 km/h sees a pedestrian with a low red health bar (5%), and the same 'MAX 40' sign, visually emphasizing the danger of speeding. Both banners prominently feature the 'Parachute' logo and the campaign hashtag '#SpeedIsNoGame'. The bottom banner also includes sponsor logos for Desjardins and CN. The visual style is flat, graphic, and uses a limited color palette of blue, gray, green, and orange to convey a clear, urgent safety message. The banners are designed to be visually striking and easily understood, likely for use in social media or print campaigns.

Visual Analysis: This image is a triptych of three sequential illustrations designed as a visual metaphor for the dangers of speeding, styled to resemble a video game interface. Each panel depicts a driver's perspective from inside a car, with a speedometer at the bottom and a health bar at the top. The first panel shows a car traveling at 80 km/h on a road marked 'MAX 80', with a full green health bar (100%) indicating safety. The second panel shows the car speeding to 100 km/h, causing the health bar to drop to 50% (orange), and a smaller '50%' indicator appears on a secondary bar, suggesting a warning state. The third panel depicts the car at 120 km/h, with the health bar critically low at 5% (red), and the car is shown overturned in a crash. The background in all panels is a stylized road with simple trees and a 'MAX 80' speed limit sign, emphasizing the violation of the speed limit as the cause of the danger. The visual style is flat, cartoonish, and uses bold colors to clearly communicate the escalating risk. The composition uses a clear left-to-right progression to illustrate a cause-and-effect narrative: safe speed → increased speed → catastrophic crash.

nodes.text: As we continued to prepare for NTDSW, another unexpected effect of COVID-19 arose: as people reduced travel due to gathering restrictions, the now-emptier roads became an inviting place for racing and stunt driving, particularly for young drivers. Our #SpeedIsNoGame messaging unfortunately became even more relevant.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: How could we make our message even stronger: that speeding was dangerous whether on our urban streets, country roads, or highways? It became clear that even if high school students were to return to in-person classes in fall 2020, there would still be restrictions on the kind of large-group assemblies and other activities where, in the past, local education and law-enforcement groups would take the Parachute NTDSW messaging directly to local students.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We knew from our student research that they trusted and listened to influencers on social media: people with large followings of fans. However, as our first focus group pointed out, something such as safety messaging would need to come from a credible source, someone accomplished rather than someone famous simply for being an online celebrity.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: Who knows better about how difficult it is to keep a car under control at fast speeds than a racing-car driver? None of the Parachute team follow racing as a sport but, as we began researching the industry, we discovered that Canadian Nicholas Latifi, then 25, was one of just 20 drivers on the elite Formula One (F1) circuit.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We made our pitch to have Latifi become our #SpeedIsNoGame spokesperson via email to his publicist based in England and, to our delight (and shock, to be frank), got an immediate and warm response, volunteering to work with us once the race team had checked out our credentials as a charity and track record in Canada. Latifi’s publicist and the Williams racing team provided photography, campaign approval and offered to promote our NTDSW messaging on Latifi’s social media channels.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: They surprised us by creating a trackside video of Latifi talking about how speed belongs on the track, but never on our streets, published on his Instagram account during NTDSW. That video has 20,000 fan views.

Visual Analysis: This is a horizontally oriented digital billboard advertisement for the 'Speed Is No Game' campaign by Parachute. The composition is split: the left side features a portrait of Canadian Formula One driver Nicholas Latifi, and the right side contains bold text and logos. Latifi is shown from the chest up, wearing a white and light blue Williams Racing racing suit with sponsor logos including 'LAVAZZA', 'Mercedes', and 'ARMC'. He has a serious, direct gaze. The background behind him is a gradient of dark blue to gray. The right side of the image has a solid black background. Dominating this area is the campaign slogan 'SPEED IS NO GAME' in large, white, bold, sans-serif font. Above it, in smaller blue text, is the phrase 'On city streets'. Below the main slogan, smaller white text provides a call to action: 'Learn about safe driving at parachuteca/speedisnogame'. At the bottom, a black banner contains the text 'Nicholas Latifi 🇨🇦 F1 Driver' in white, followed by sponsor logos: 'Sponsored by Desjardins Insurance' and the 'Parachute' organization logo (a green parachute shape). The overall visual style is clean, high-contrast, and impactful, designed for maximum readability and brand recognition. The image is clearly a promotional asset for a public safety campaign.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: In fall 2020, Canadian rail company CN became an additional sponsor for NTDSW, allowing us to partner with You Tube influencers who are content creators with a teen audience following to reach more youth directly in Canada. Composer and travel video producer Andrew Gunnadie (aka Gunnarolla) has 91,700 YouTube subscribers: we hired him to create an original video, using our key safety messaging but in his own style and published to his followers.

nodes.title: Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Taking the high road: campaigning for safe driving  Summary
nodes.text: We also partnered with Québec Youtuber, Élie Pilon, with 66,700 followers. Pilon’s videos are long, by usual social media standards, but his followers are keen to enjoy his rapid-fire rant-style musings on a wide range of topics: this time, about speeding on our roads. His video, Les roadtrips en 4 étapes had 20,600 fan views during NTDSW and has drawn another 7,000 views in the months since.

The overall visual style is clean and impactful, designed to convey a serious safety message through the authority of a well-known athlete. nodes.title: Sensitivity of implicit evaluations to accurate and erroneous propositional inferences  ARTICLEINFO  ABSTRACT
nodes.text: Explicit (directly measured) evaluations are widely assumed to be sensitive to logical structure.However, whether implicit (indirectly measured) evaluations are uniquely sensitive to co-occurrence information or can also reflect logical structure has been a mater of theoretical debate.To test these competing ideas,participants $( N = 3 9 2 8 )$ completed a learning phase consisting of a series of two-step trials.In step 1,one or more conditional statements $\left( \mathsf { A } \to \mathsf { B } \right)$ containing novel targets co-occurring with valenced adjectives (e.g.,"if you see a blue square, Ibbonif is sincere") were presented.In step 2,a disambiguating stimulus,.g.,blue square (A)or gray blob (-A) wasrevealed. $\mathrm { C o }$ -occurrence information,disambiguating stimuli,or both were varied between conditions to enable investigating the unique and joint efects of each.Across studies,the combination of conditional statements and disambiguating stimuli licensed diferent normatively accurate inferences.In Study 1,participants were prompted to use modus ponens (inferring B from $\mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ and A).In Studies 2-4,the information did not license accurate inferences,but some participants made inferential errors: afrming the consequent (inferrig A from $\mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ and B; Study 2) or denying the antecedent (inferring $\lnot \mathbf { B }$ from $\mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ and $\neg \mathbf { A } ;$ Studies 3A,3B,and 4). Bayesian modeling using ordinal constraints oncondition means yielded consistent evidenceforthe sensitivity of both explicit (self-report)and implicit (IATand AMP)evaluations to the (correctly or erroneously inferred truth value of propositions.Together,these data suggest that implicit evaluations,similar to their explicit counterparts,can reflect logical structure.

nodes.title: Sensitivity of implicit evaluations to accurate and erroneous propositional inferences  ARTICLEINFO  ABSTRACT
nodes.text: To obtain rewards and avoid punishments,organisms must maintain accurate representations of their environment.For humans,who live in societies of unprecedented scale and complexity,interacting with social partners carries paramount importance for success and even survival.As such,to adequately navigate the social world,people require up-to-date knowledge of whom they can trust and whom they ought to mistrust. Accordingly,investigating representations of the goodness or badness of social entities,as well as the origins of such representations,has had a pride of place in scientific psychology since the very inception of the field (e.g., Alport, 1935; Eagly & Chaiken,1993; McGuire,1985; Wood, 2000).

nodes.title: Sensitivity of implicit evaluations to accurate and erroneous propositional inferences  ARTICLEINFO  ABSTRACT
nodes.text: In the present work we explore how social evaluations are acquired and updated, with special focus on implicit evaluations (Devine,1989; Fazio, Sanbonmatsu， Powell， & Kardes,1986; Greenwald & Banaji, 1995),i.e.,evaluations whose presence is inferred without asking participants to intentionally reflect on the to-be-measured mental content.

nodes.title: Sensitivity of implicit evaluations to accurate and erroneous propositional inferences  ARTICLEINFO  ABSTRACT
nodes.text: Under this definition, implicit evaluations differ from their explicit counterparts in features of the measurement context,with the former relying on indirect indices of underlying knowledge (such as response latencies) and the latter on direct indices of underlying knowledge (such as different forms of self-report).Whether implicit and explicit evaluations also differ from each other more deeply,especially in the types of learning and information to which they are sensitive,has beena matter of debate both in psychology (e.g.,De Houwer, 2014; DeCoster, Banner, Smith，& Semin，2006;Gawronski & Bodenhausen，2006; Hughes, Barnes-Holmes,& De Houwer, 2011; Kruglanski & Gigerenzer, 2011; Kurdi & Dunham, 2020; Mitchell, De Houwer,& Lovibond, 2009; Smith & DeCoster, 200o; Strack & Deutsch, 2004) and philosophy (e.g., Gendler, 2008; Levy, 2014; Madva, 2016; Mandelbaum, 2016).

nodes.title: Sensitivity of implicit evaluations to accurate and erroneous propositional inferences  ARTICLEINFO  ABSTRACT
nodes.text: Specifically,among many other modalities of learning, both explicit and implicit evaluations have been shown to respond to verbal statements about social targets (e.g., Cone & Ferguson, 2O15; Kurdi & Banaji, 2017，2019； Peters & Gawronski，2011；Rydell， McConnell， Strain, Claypool, & Hugenberg, 2Oo6). For instance, exposure to a statement such as “All Niffians are good and allLaapians are bad"(Kurdi & Banaji, 2017; Study 6C) can result in the updating of both explicit and implicit evaluations of these novel targets in the corresponding directions. However,results of this kind leave open the question of what specific features of verbal material social evaluations are responsive to and whether such features are the same or different depending on whether evaluations are measured explicitly or implicitly.This is the question that we take up in the present work.
